facts.text: character introduced
facts.argument: "Alice was beginning to get very tired of sitting by her sister on the bank..."

facts.text: Curious and impulsive, she chases the talking White Rabbit, follows it down a large rabbit-hole, and begins falling down a very deep well.
facts.argument: "burning with curiosity, she ran... just in time to see it pop down a large rabbit-hole... down went Alice... falling down a very deep well."

facts.text: On a hot day she sits by her sister, bored and sleepy, briefly peeps at her sister’s pictureless book and considers making a daisy-chain.
facts.argument: "the hot day made her feel very sleepy and stupid"; "peeped into the book her sister was reading"; "it had no pictures or conversations"; "considering... making a daisy-chain"

facts.text: While falling down the well, Alice remains calm and curious: she notes cupboards/bookshelves with maps and pictures, takes an empty 'ORANGE MARMALADE' jar but carefully replaces it in a cupboard, talks aloud to herself, rehearses schoolroom knowledge (distance to Earth's center, latitude/longitude) despite not fully understanding, and muses about falling through to places like New Zealand or Australia (calling the people the 'Antipathies').
facts.argument: She observes shelves with maps/pictures; takes an empty marmalade jar and “managed to put it into one of the cupboards”; says aloud she’s fallen “four thousand miles” and wonders about “Latitude or Longitude”; jokes about the “Antipathies” and asks if it’s “New Zealand or Australia.”

facts.text: Alice falls a long way, lands unharmed on a heap of sticks and dry leaves, and continues pursuing the White Rabbit into a long, low, lamp-lit hall.
facts.argument: “down she came upon a heap of sticks and dry leaves… the fall was over… the White Rabbit was still in sight… she found herself in a long, low hall… lit up by a row of lamps”

facts.text: While falling, Alice grows sleepy, repetitively wonders if cats eat bats (and vice versa), dozes, and dreams of walking with Dinah and asking if she ever ate a bat.
facts.argument: “Do cats eat bats? … Do bats eat cats? … she was dozing off… dream… walking hand in hand with Dinah… ‘did you ever eat a bat?’”

facts.text: Alice discovers a hidden little door behind a curtain; the tiny golden key from the glass table fits it, revealing a passage to a lovely garden, but she is too large to enter and wishes she could "shut up like a telescope" to fit.
facts.argument: "behind it was a little door... she tried the little golden key in the lock, and ... it fitted!... looked along the passage into the loveliest garden... she could not even get her head through... 'Oh, how I wish I could shut up like a telescope!'"

facts.text: Alice finds a glass table with a tiny golden key and later a labeled bottle reading "DRINK ME" that was not there before.
facts.argument: "a little three-legged table, all made of solid glass ... a tiny golden key"; later: "this time she found a little bottle on it ('which certainly was not here before') ... label... 'DRINK ME'"

facts.text: Alice's mindset shifts toward accepting the impossible; she thinks very few things are really impossible after recent strange events and imagines shrinking like a telescope.
facts.argument: "so many out-of-the-way things had happened lately, that Alice had begun to think that very few things indeed were really impossible"; "Oh, how I wish I could shut up like a telescope!"

facts.text: After drinking from a bottle labeled 'Drink me' (not marked 'poison'), she shrinks to about ten inches high.
facts.argument: "This bottle was not marked 'poison'... she very soon finished it off." / "She was now only ten inches high."

facts.text: She cautiously checks for a 'poison' label and recalls safety lessons before tasting the 'Drink me' bottle.
facts.argument: "No, I'll look first ... and see whether it's marked 'poison' or not"; she remembered rules from stories and friends.

facts.text: Now the right size for the little door to the garden, she waits to see if she'll shrink further, nervous she might 'go out altogether, like a candle.'
facts.argument: "She was now only ten inches high," "now the right size for going through the little door... First, however, she waited... she felt a little nervous... might end... in my going out altogether, like a candle. "

facts.text: She admonishes herself and even pretends to be two people; she gives herself strong advice, scolds herself to tears, and once tried to box her own ears for cheating herself in a solo croquet game.
facts.argument: "'Come, there’s no use in crying like that!' said Alice to herself ... she scolded herself so severely as to bring tears ... once ... trying to box her own ears ... playing against herself ... fond of pretending to be two people."

facts.text: She discovers a small cake labeled 'EAT ME' in a glass box under the table and decides to eat it to change size so she can reach the key or creep under the door to get into the garden.
facts.argument: "a very small cake ... on which the words 'EAT ME' were ... 'if it makes me grow larger, I can reach the key; and if it makes me grow smaller, I can creep under the door; so either way I’ll get into the garden'"

facts.text: She forgot the little golden key on the table and, being too small to reach it through the glass, tried and failed to climb the slippery table leg before sitting down to cry.
facts.argument: "she found she had forgotten the little golden key ... she could not possibly reach it ... tried ... to climb up one of the legs of the table, but it was too slippery ... sat down and cried."

facts.text: After finishing the cake, Alice suddenly grows dramatically—“opening out like the largest telescope”—until she is more than nine feet high, strikes the hall roof, then takes the little golden key and hurries to the garden door.
facts.argument: “now I’m opening out like the largest telescope…,” “she was now more than nine feet high,” and “she at once took up the little golden key and hurried off to the garden door.”

facts.text: In surprise she exclaims “Curiouser and curiouser!” and momentarily forgets proper English.
facts.argument: “Curiouser and curiouser!” … “she was so much surprised, that for the moment she quite forgot how to speak good English”.

facts.text: She whimsically addresses her own feet, bids them goodbye, and plans to send them new boots every Christmas by carrier, even imagining an address label.
facts.argument: “Good-bye, feet!” … “They must go by the carrier,” and the mock address “Alice’s Right Foot, Esq., Hearthrug, near the Fender (with Alice’s love).”

facts.text: After eating a small piece of cake, she is disappointed to remain the same size, having come to expect strange changes in Wonderland.
facts.argument: “she remained the same size… Alice had got so much into the way of expecting nothing but out-of-the-way things… it seemed dull… for life to go on in the common way.”

facts.text: Too big to fit through the door to the garden; can only look through with one eye while lying down, and getting through seems more hopeless than ever.
facts.argument: “lying down on one side, to look through into the garden with one eye; but to get through was more hopeless than ever”

facts.text: Scolds herself for crying but continues, shedding so many tears that she creates a large pool about four inches deep reaching half down the hall.
facts.argument: “You ought to be ashamed… Stop this moment,” but “she went on… shedding gallons of tears… a large pool… about four inches deep and reaching half down the hall.”

facts.text: Picks up the White Rabbit’s dropped white kid gloves and large fan; fans herself because the hall is very hot.
facts.argument: “Alice took up the fan and gloves… as the hall was very hot, she kept fanning herself.”

facts.text: Questions her identity, wondering if she was changed in the night and asking, “Who in the world am I?” while comparing herself to other children of her age.
facts.argument: “I wonder if I’ve been changed in the night?… Who in the world am I?… thinking over all the children she knew… to see if she could have been changed for any of them.”

facts.text: Questions her identity, comparing herself to Ada and Mabel; resolves to stay 'down here' if she is Mabel.
facts.argument: Contrasts herself with Ada and Mabel and says, “if I’m Mabel, I’ll stay down here.”

facts.text: Her lessons come out wrong and her voice sounds hoarse and strange; she recites a distorted poem and becomes tearful from loneliness.
facts.argument: “four times five is twelve... London is the capital of Paris...” “her voice sounded hoarse and strange... words did not come the same” and “her eyes filled with tears... tired of being all alone.”

facts.text: Discovers the fan she is holding makes her shrink rapidly; drops it just in time to avoid shrinking away.
facts.argument: "she soon found out that the cause of this was the fan she was holding, and she dropped it hastily, just in time to avoid shrinking away altogether."

facts.text: After shrinking to about two feet high, she returns to the little door but it is shut; later slips and ends up swimming in a pool of her own tears, fearing she might drown in them.
facts.argument: "now about two feet high"; "the little door was shut again"; "splash! she was up to her chin in salt water... she soon made out that she was in the pool of tears"; "I shall be... drowned in my own tears!"

facts.text: Has been to the seaside once; associates English coasts with bathing machines, children digging, lodging houses, and a railway station.
facts.argument: "Alice had been to the seaside once in her life... wherever you go to on the English coast you find... bathing machines... children... lodging houses... a railway station."

facts.text: Alice attempts to communicate with animals, trying English and then French based on a grammar lesson, and apologizes for upsetting the Mouse.
facts.argument: She thinks “it can talk,” says “O Mouse...,” then tries “Où est ma chatte?” and apologizes: “I beg your pardon!”

facts.text: Leads the party from the pool to the shore and soon speaks familiarly with the gathered birds and animals, as if long acquainted.
facts.argument: "Alice led the way, and the whole party swam to the shore"; later, it seemed natural to be "talking familiarly with them, as if she had known them all her life."

facts.text: Produces a box of comfits from her pocket and hands them round as prizes; also has a thimble in her pocket (which the Dodo claims for her prize).
facts.argument: "pulled out a box of comfits ... and handed them round as prizes"; "Only a thimble," said Alice sadly.

facts.text: Politely went along with an absurd ceremony, bowing and accepting the thimble while keeping a solemn face.
facts.argument: "Alice thought the whole thing very absurd... she... bowed, and took the thimble, looking as solemn as she could."

facts.text: Tends to take wordplay literally, confusing 'tale' with 'tail' and referring to the 'fifth bend' of the Mouse's tail.
facts.argument: "It is a long tail, certainly..." and later, "you had got to the fifth bend, I think?"

facts.text: Frightened by the White Rabbit’s angry order, Alice runs in the direction he points and arrives at a neat little house marked 'W. RABBIT'.
facts.argument: “Alice was so much frightened that she ran off at once in the direction it pointed… she came upon a neat little house… with the name ‘W. RABBIT.’”

facts.text: Mistaken by the White Rabbit for his housemaid Mary Ann.
facts.argument: “He took me for his housemaid,” Alice thinks after the Rabbit orders her about.

facts.text: Entered the White Rabbit’s house and went upstairs to fetch his fan and white kid gloves, taking a fan and one pair from a tidy room.
facts.argument: "She went in ... hurried upstairs ... on it ... a fan and two or three pairs of tiny white kid gloves: she took up the fan and a pair of the gloves."

facts.text: Drank from an unlabeled bottle in the Rabbit’s room and grew rapidly until she filled the room, pressing against the ceiling and unable to get out the door.
facts.argument: "There was no label ... she uncorked it ... before she had drunk half the bottle, she found her head pressing against the ceiling ... As it is, I can’t get out at the door."

facts.text: While inside the White Rabbit’s house, Alice grew so enormous she had one arm out the window and one foot up the chimney; the little bottle’s magic finished and she stopped growing but remained stuck and uncomfortable.
facts.argument: “she put one arm out of the window, and one foot up the chimney… the little magic bottle had now had its full effect, and she grew no larger… very uncomfortable… no sort of chance of her ever getting out of the room again”

facts.text: While stuck in the Rabbit’s house, Alice holds a self-dialogue, resolves there ought to be a book about her (and that she’ll write it when grown up), and muses about never aging versus having endless lessons.
facts.argument: “There ought to be a book written about me… when I grow up, I’ll write one… shall I never get any older… never to be an old woman… always to have lessons… she… making quite a conversation of it altogether.”

facts.text: Threatens to set her cat Dinah on the White Rabbit and his helpers if they burn the house; eats one of the thrown pebble-cakes to shrink small enough to escape; resolves to regain her normal size and find the lovely garden.
facts.argument: Calls out "If you do, I'll set Dinah at you!" Notices pebbles turn into cakes, eats one and shrinks, runs into a wood, planning to grow to right size and reach the garden.

facts.text: Alice seeks a way to change size back to 'grow up again' and considers eating or drinking something; she finds a large mushroom and discovers a blue caterpillar atop it.
facts.argument: Alice says she needs to 'grow up again' and looks for something to eat or drink; she notices a large mushroom and sees a caterpillar on top.

facts.text: Struggles with frequent size changes and memory lapses in Wonderland; even familiar verses come out wrong.
facts.argument: "I don’t keep the same size for ten minutes together!" and "I’ve tried to say 'How doth the little busy bee,' but it all came different!"

facts.text: Recites the poem 'You are old, Father William' at the Caterpillar's command, then timidly admits her version has altered words.
facts.argument: Alice folded her hands and began… “Not quite right… some of the words have got altered.”

facts.text: Currently about three inches tall, she dislikes the size and wishes to be a little larger. She breaks off two pieces of the mushroom to test its sides; nibbling the right-hand bit makes her shrink so fast her chin strikes her foot, showing that side makes her smaller.
facts.argument: "three inches is such a wretched height"; she "broke off a bit of the edge with each hand" and after nibbling the right-hand bit "felt a violent blow underneath her chin: it had struck her foot!"

facts.text: Alice eats more mushroom, shrinks rapidly, and then grows an extremely long, flexible neck that can bend like a serpent.
facts.argument: She ate some of the other bit; soon her head is free with an immense length of neck that bends easily in any direction, like a serpent.

facts.text: Alice is described as a very truthful child and admits she has tasted eggs.
facts.argument: Narration: “Alice, who was a very truthful child”; Alice: “I have tasted eggs, certainly.”

facts.text: Uses the mushroom pieces to adjust her size—returning to her usual height—then shrinks herself to nine inches before approaching a four-foot-high house so as not to frighten its residents; reaffirms her goal to enter the 'beautiful garden.'
facts.argument: "nibbling first at one and then at the other... bringing herself down to her usual height"; "the next thing is, to get into that beautiful garden"; "it'll never do to come upon them this size"; "till she had brought herself down to nine inches high."

facts.text: Moved by concern, Alice carries the Duchess’s baby away to save it, but abandons it when it turns into a pig.
facts.argument: “If I don’t take this child away… wouldn’t it be murder…?” … “it was… a pig… So she set the little creature down.”

facts.text: Wants to play croquet with the Queen but has not been invited yet.
facts.argument: Alice: “I should like it very much… but I haven’t been invited yet.”

facts.text: Gives up on the Hatter’s riddle and criticizes asking riddles with no answers as a waste of time.
facts.argument: “No, I give it up… what’s the answer?” … “you might do something better with the time… than waste it in asking riddles that have no answers.”

facts.text: She is described as always taking a great interest in questions of eating and drinking.
facts.argument: Narration: Alice “always took a great interest in questions of eating and drinking.”

facts.text: Uses a saved piece of mushroom to shrink to about a foot and finally gains entry to the beautiful garden via the small door.
facts.argument: “nibbling at the mushroom… till she was about a foot high… then… she found herself at last in the beautiful garden”

facts.text: Alice chooses not to prostrate herself at the procession, stands her ground, and boldly contradicts the Queen, thinking the court are only a pack of cards.
facts.argument: "she stood still where she was"; "'they’re only a pack of cards'"; "'Nonsense!' said Alice"

facts.text: Finds the Queen’s croquet game very difficult, struggling to manage a live flamingo mallet and hedgehog ball amid uneven ground and moving soldier-arches.
facts.argument: She laughs as the flamingo looks up at her; the hedgehog unrolls and crawls away; ridges/furrows obstruct; soldier-arches keep walking off.

facts.text: Alice endures discomfort to avoid being rude, staying close to the Duchess despite disliking it.
facts.argument: “she did not like to be rude, so she bore it as well as she could,” though the Duchess’s sharp chin on her shoulder was uncomfortable.

facts.text: Alice muses that when she is a Duchess she will ban pepper from her kitchen, inventing a ‘rule’ that pepper makes people hot-tempered, vinegar makes them sour, camomile bitter, and barley-sugar makes children sweet-tempered.
facts.argument: “When I’m a Duchess… I won’t have any pepper… Maybe it’s always pepper that makes people hot-tempered… and vinegar… sour… camomile… bitter… barley-sugar… make children sweet-tempered.”

facts.text: Alice learns of the Mock Turtle from the Queen and agrees to go hear his history despite not knowing what it is.
facts.argument: “Have you seen the Mock Turtle yet?” … “I don’t even know what a Mock Turtle is.” … “Come on, then,” said the Queen, “and he shall tell you his history.”

facts.text: Has been to a day-school and learned French and music.
facts.argument: “I’ve been to a day-school, too… we learned French and music.”

facts.text: When made to recite, Alice delivers a muddled version beginning “’Tis the voice of the Lobster,” influenced by the Lobster Quadrille; she feels ordered about like at school and continues in a trembling voice.
facts.argument: “she got up, and began to repeat it… ‘’Tis the voice of the Lobster…’”; “How the creatures order one about… I might as well be at school”; “she went on in a trembling voice.”

facts.text: Attends her first court of justice; identifies the judge and jurors from what she has read in books.
facts.argument: "Alice had never been in a court of justice before"; she thinks, "That's the judge" and "those twelve creatures ... I suppose they are the jurors."

facts.text: Begins growing larger again during the trial and decides to remain seated as long as there is room.
facts.argument: "she was beginning to grow larger again... decided to remain where she was as long as there was room."

facts.text: Called as a witness; having recently grown larger, she jumps up and accidentally tips over the jury-box, then hastily collects and replaces the jurors.
facts.argument: “‘Here!’ cried Alice … forgetting … how large she had grown … she tipped over the jury-box … and began picking them up again …”

facts.text: Publicly challenges the Queen’s claim that the unsigned verses prove the Knave’s guilt, insisting the content be read first.
facts.argument: Alice: “It proves nothing of the sort! Why, you don’t even know what they’re about!”

facts.text: At the trial she grows very large, confidently interrupts the King, declares the verses meaningless, and offers sixpence to any juror who can explain them.
facts.argument: "she had grown so large ... that she wasn’t a bit afraid of interrupting him"; "I’ll give him sixpence... I don’t believe there’s an atom of meaning in it."

facts.text: Wakes from Wonderland, realizing the adventures were a dream; she recounts them to her sister and is told to go to tea.
facts.argument: "found herself lying on the bank, with her head in the lap of her sister"; "Oh, I’ve had such a curious dream!"; "now run in to your tea; it’s getting late."

facts.text: Alice regards her Wonderland experiences as a dream and runs off thinking it had been a wonderful dream.
facts.argument: "So Alice got up and ran off, thinking... what a wonderful dream it had been."

facts.text: Her sister imagines her future as a grown woman who retains her childhood’s loving heart and tells stories to children—perhaps even the Wonderland dream—sharing in their simple sorrows and joys.
facts.argument: “She pictured… her little sister… be herself a grown woman… keep… the simple and loving heart… gather… other little children… make their eyes bright… perhaps even with the dream of Wonderland… feel… their simple sorrows… pleasure in… simple joys.”

facts.text: character introduced
facts.argument: "suddenly a White Rabbit with pink eyes ran close by her"; it speaks and checks a watch.

facts.text: Anxiously talks about being late, takes a watch from its waistcoat-pocket, and hurries into a rabbit-hole.
facts.argument: "Oh dear! Oh dear! I shall be late!"; "took a watch out of its waistcoat-pocket... and then hurried on... pop down a large rabbit-hole"

facts.text: Has pink eyes and wears a waistcoat with a pocket for a watch.
facts.argument: "a White Rabbit with pink eyes"; "waistcoat-pocket"

facts.text: While hurrying ahead of Alice, exclaims, “Oh my ears and whiskers, how late it’s getting!” and disappears around a corner into a long passage/hall.
facts.argument: “the White Rabbit was still in sight… ‘Oh my ears and whiskers, how late it’s getting!’ … she turned the corner, but the Rabbit was no longer to be seen”

facts.text: Returns dressed formally with white kid gloves and a large fan, rushing and muttering about the Duchess being angry if kept waiting.
facts.argument: “the White Rabbit returning, splendidly dressed, with a pair of white kid gloves in one hand and a large fan in the other… ‘Oh! the Duchess… won’t she be savage if I’ve kept her waiting!’”

facts.text: Startled by Alice’s timid address, he drops the gloves and fan and flees into the darkness.
facts.argument: At “If you please, sir—” the Rabbit “started violently, dropped the white kid gloves and the fan, and skurried away….”

facts.text: Has little white kid gloves; Alice finds she has accidentally put one on.
facts.argument: "she was surprised to see that she had put on one of the Rabbit’s little white kid gloves"

facts.text: The White Rabbit anxiously searches for his lost fan and white kid gloves; he fears the Duchess will have him executed if he fails; he maintains a house marked 'W. RABBIT' and has a housemaid named Mary Ann.
facts.argument: “She’ll get me executed”; “Where can I have dropped them”; brass plate with 'W. RABBIT'; “Why, Mary Ann… fetch me a pair of gloves and a fan!”

facts.text: His house contains a tidy room with a table in the window holding a fan and several pairs of tiny white kid gloves, from which Alice took a pair.
facts.argument: "a tidy little room with a table in the window, and on it ... a fan and two or three pairs of tiny white kid gloves"

facts.text: At his house, the White Rabbit calls out for Mary Ann to fetch his gloves and comes up the stairs, identified by the patter of his feet.
facts.argument: “‘Mary Ann! Mary Ann!’ said the voice. ‘Fetch me my gloves this moment!’ Then came a little pattering of feet on the stairs.”

facts.text: Attempts to enter his own house by the window after failing at the door; encounters Alice’s giant arm blocking the window and orders Pat to remove it.
facts.argument: “I’ll go round and get in at the window.”; Rabbit angry: “What’s that in the window?”; “go and take it away!”

facts.text: Present outside his house with a group of helpers; exerts authority as 'the master' during efforts to deal with the giant arm in his window.
facts.argument: Multiple voices coordinate ladders and ropes; someone says, “the master says you’re to go down the chimney,” and later the Rabbit’s voice directs, “Catch him... Hold up his head—Brandy now…”

facts.text: Proposes burning down his own house to deal with Alice inside and directs helpers to throw pebbles through the window.
facts.argument: "We must burn the house down!" and "A barrowful will do" followed by a shower of pebbles at the window.

facts.text: Appears among the Queen’s guests in the royal procession, talking hurriedly and smiling at everything, and passes without noticing Alice.
facts.argument: “Among them Alice recognised the White Rabbit: it was talking in a hurried nervous manner, smiling at everything … and went by without noticing her.”

facts.text: Speaks in a timid, hurried whisper around the Queen, peeping anxiously into Alice’s face and cautioning her to hush so the Queen won’t hear.
facts.argument: "a timid voice" ... "peeping anxiously into her face" ... "Oh, hush! ... The Queen will hear you!"

facts.text: Serves as a court herald/clerk, attending near the King with a trumpet and a scroll of parchment.
facts.argument: "near the King was the White Rabbit, with a trumpet in one hand, and a scroll of parchment in the other."

facts.text: Acts as court herald: calls for silence, blows a trumpet, reads the parchment accusation, and summons the first witness.
facts.argument: The White Rabbit blows three blasts, unrolls the parchment, reads the accusation, calls for silence, and summons the first witness.

facts.text: Acts as court clerk, fumbling the witness list and calling Alice as the next witness.
facts.argument: “Alice watched the White Rabbit as he fumbled over the list … the White Rabbit read out … the name ‘Alice!’”

facts.text: Acts as court reader and evidence-presenter at the trial; produces a paper he thought a letter, reveals it is a set of verses, and puts on spectacles to read.
facts.argument: “this paper has just been picked up” … “It isn’t a letter, after all: it’s a set of verses.” … “The White Rabbit put on his spectacles… ‘Where shall I begin?’”

summaries.text: A white rabbit with pink eyes who speaks, carries a watch in a waistcoat-pocket, and hurries past Alice into a rabbit-hole.

facts.text: character introduced
facts.argument: "sitting by her sister on the bank"; sister is reading a book without pictures or conversations.

facts.text: She reads a book without pictures or conversations while sitting with Alice on the bank.
facts.argument: "sitting by her sister on the bank"; the book "had no pictures or conversations"

facts.text: Gently wakes Alice, brushes leaves from her face, listens to Alice’s dream, kisses her, and sends her in to tea.
facts.argument: "Wake up, Alice dear!... gently brushing away some dead leaves"; she "kissed her, and said... now run in to your tea."

facts.text: After Alice leaves, she sits watching the setting sun and drifts into a daydream in which the creatures from Alice’s adventures seem alive around her (White Rabbit, Mouse, March Hare and friends at tea, Queen’s orders, pig-baby sneezing, Gryphon shriek, Lizard’s squeaking slate-pencil, suppressed guinea-pigs, Mock Turtle’s sobs).
facts.argument: "her sister... began dreaming... the whole place around her became alive with the strange creatures of her little sister’s dream" followed by the list.

facts.text: After Alice leaves, she sits with closed eyes, half-believing in Wonderland, translating its sounds into pastoral reality, then envisions Alice grown, keeping her childhood’s loving heart and telling stories to children, perhaps even the Wonderland dream.
facts.argument: “So she sat on, with closed eyes… teacups… to sheep-bells… Queen’s… to the voice of the shepherd boy… Lastly, she pictured… her little sister… a grown woman… keep… the loving heart… gather… other little children… perhaps even with the dream of Wonderland.”

summaries.text: Alice’s sister, reading a book without pictures or conversations while sitting with Alice on a bank.

Alice's sister, often seen reading a book without pictures, gently wakes Alice and listens to her dreams. After Alice leaves, she daydreams about the whimsical creatures from Alice's adventures, reflecting her connection to her sister's imaginative world.

Alice's sister, often seen reading a book without pictures, gently wakes Alice and listens to her dreams. After Alice departs, she daydreams about whimsical creatures from Wonderland, reflecting her deep connection to Alice's imaginative world.

facts.text: character introduced
facts.argument: “Dinah was the cat.” Alice thinks about Dinah missing her and her saucer of milk.

facts.text: Alice associates Dinah with hunting mice, wonders if cats eat bats, and expects someone to remember Dinah’s saucer of milk at tea-time.
facts.argument: “Dinah’ll miss me… I hope they’ll remember her saucer of milk at tea-time… there are no mice in the air… you might catch a bat… do cats eat bats?”

facts.text: Alice describes Dinah as a dear, quiet cat who purrs by the fire, licks her paws and washes her face, is soft to nurse, and is very good at catching mice.
facts.argument: "she sits purring... licking her paws and washing her face... nice soft thing to nurse... such a capital one for catching mice"

facts.text: Perceived as unpopular among Wonderland’s creatures, prompting Alice’s lament that no one likes her there.
facts.argument: Alice: “Nobody seems to like her, down here.”

summaries.text: Alice’s pet cat; associated with a saucer of milk at tea-time and thought to catch mice (per Alice).

Dinah is Alice's beloved pet cat, known for her quiet demeanor and soft fur. Associated with tea-time and a saucer of milk, she is thought to be skilled at catching mice, and Alice fondly describes her as a dear companion who enjoys purring by the fire.

facts.text: character introduced
facts.argument: The White Rabbit mutters, “Oh! the Duchess, the Duchess! Oh! won’t she be savage if I’ve kept her waiting!”

facts.text: The Duchess is feared as harsh and powerful; the White Rabbit believes she could have him executed over missing items.
facts.argument: White Rabbit: “She’ll get me executed, as sure as ferrets are ferrets!”

facts.text: Seen sitting on a three-legged stool in her smoky kitchen, nursing a baby; sneezes due to pepper in the air.
facts.argument: "the Duchess was sitting on a three-legged stool... nursing a baby"; "Even the Duchess sneezed occasionally"

facts.text: Dislikes dealing with numbers or arithmetic.
facts.argument: The Duchess: "I never could abide figures!"

facts.text: Handles her baby roughly, shaking and tossing it while singing an abusive lullaby about beating him when he sneezes.
facts.argument: She shakes the child at the end of every line and "kept tossing the baby violently up and down"; lyrics: "Speak roughly to your little boy... And beat him when he sneezes."

facts.text: Reported by the White Rabbit to be under sentence of execution for boxing the Queen of Hearts’ ears (after arriving late).
facts.argument: "She’s under sentence of execution." ... "She boxed the Queen’s ears— ... she came rather late"

facts.text: At the croquet ground, the Duchess presses very close to Alice, digging her sharp little chin into Alice’s shoulder; she is described as very ugly and is strongly fond of finding a ‘moral’ in everything.
facts.argument: “the Duchess was very ugly… exactly the right height to rest her chin upon Alice’s shoulder… an uncomfortably sharp chin… ‘Everything’s got a moral, if only you can find it.’”

facts.text: Shows an affable, moralizing demeanor with Alice: flatters her and readily agrees to everything she says, delivers "morals" (e.g., 'Birds of a feather...', 'The more there is of mine...', 'Be what you would seem to be...'), and is physically intrusive, digging her sharp little chin into Alice; considers putting an arm round Alice’s waist but refrains for fear of the flamingo biting.
facts.argument: "who seemed ready to agree to everything that Alice said"; "And the moral of that is—"; "with another dig of her sharp little chin"; "I’m doubtful about the temper of your flamingo... Shall I try the experiment?"

summaries.text: A figure the White Rabbit fears keeping waiting; referenced as likely to be angry if delayed.
The Duchess is a feared and powerful figure in Wonderland, known for her harsh demeanor. The White Rabbit dreads keeping her waiting, believing she could have him executed for missing items.

The Duchess is a feared and powerful figure in Wonderland, known for her harsh demeanor and her ability to execute those who displease her, like the White Rabbit. Often seen nursing a baby in her smoky kitchen, she is characterized by her sneezing from the pepper in the air.

The Duchess is a feared and powerful figure in Wonderland, known for her harsh demeanor and ability to execute those who displease her, like the White Rabbit. Often seen nursing a baby in her smoky kitchen, she sneezes from pepper and sings abusive lullabies.

The Duchess is a feared and powerful figure in Wonderland, known for her harsh demeanor and abusive lullabies. Often seen nursing a baby in her smoky kitchen, she is notorious for her readiness to execute those who displease her, like the White Rabbit.

facts.text: character introduced
facts.argument: Alice says, “I’m sure I’m not Ada, for her hair goes in such long ringlets,” distinguishing Ada by her long ringlets.

facts.text: Known to Alice for her long ringlets; Alice denies being Ada.
facts.argument: “I’m sure I’m not Ada... for her hair goes in such long ringlets.”

summaries.text: A girl known to Alice, identified by her long ringlets; Alice compares herself against Ada when questioning her identity.

facts.text: character introduced
facts.argument: Alice contrasts herself with Mabel, noting Mabel knows very little and has a poky little house with few toys and many lessons.

facts.text: Per Alice, knows very little; associated with a poky little house, few toys, and many lessons.
facts.argument: “I can’t be Mabel, for I know all sorts of things, and she... knows very little... poky little house... next to no toys... ever so many lessons.”

summaries.text: A girl known to Alice, characterized as knowing very little; associated with a poky house, few toys, and many lessons. Alice fears she might have been changed into Mabel.

facts.text: character introduced
facts.argument: Alice swims toward splashing and sees it is “only a mouse that had slipped in like herself,” which later speaks: “Not like cats!”

facts.text: The Mouse is frightened by mention of cats and protests loudly when Alice brings up one.
facts.argument: After “Où est ma chatte?” the Mouse “gave a sudden leap... quiver[ed] with fright” and cried, “Not like cats!”

facts.text: The Mouse and its family strongly hate cats and do not want to hear even the name mentioned; it is also frightened or offended by dogs.
facts.argument: "Our family always hated cats... Don't let me hear the name again!" and it swims away when Alice praises a dog.

facts.text: Assumes an authority role among the wet creatures, ordering them to sit and promising to make them dry.
facts.argument: "the Mouse, who seemed to be a person of authority among them, called out, 'Sit down, all of you... I'll soon make you dry enough!'"

facts.text: Leads the drying attempt by reciting a very 'dry' English history lesson, which it calls the driest thing it knows; checks on Alice's progress while reading.
facts.argument: "Ahem! ... This is the driest thing I know... 'William the Conqueror...'" and later, "How are you getting on now, my dear?"

facts.text: Introduced its history as "a long and a sad tale" and began reciting a rhymed story about Fury prosecuting a mouse.
facts.argument: "Mine is a long and a sad tale!" followed by the verse beginning "Fury said to a mouse..."

summaries.text: A talking mouse who slipped into the pool and swims near Alice; easily frightened and vehemently dislikes cats.

A talking mouse who is easily frightened, vehemently dislikes cats, and protests loudly at their mention. Introduced in 'Alice's Adventures in Wonderland', he swims near Alice and shares a strong aversion to dogs as well.

The Mouse is a talking, easily frightened character from 'Alice's Adventures in Wonderland'. He vehemently dislikes cats and dogs, protesting loudly at their mention, and assumes a leadership role among the wet creatures, directing them to sit and dry off.

facts.text: character introduced
facts.argument: "there were a Duck" among the creatures in the pool who swam to shore with Alice.

facts.text: Takes things literally and humorously, saying when it "finds" something it's usually a frog or a worm, while questioning the Mouse's phrasing.
facts.argument: Duck: "I know what 'it' means ... it's generally a frog or a worm. The question is, what did the archbishop find?"

summaries.text: A wet bird from the pool who joins the group on the bank seeking to get dry.

facts.text: character introduced
facts.argument: "there were a Duck and a Dodo" among the creatures in the pool who swam to shore with Alice.

facts.text: Speaks in formal, parliamentary tones and proposes a Caucus-race as a more energetic remedy to get everyone dry, moving to adjourn the meeting.
facts.argument: "I move that the meeting adjourn, for the immediate adoption of more energetic remedies—" and "the best thing to get us dry would be a Caucus-race."

facts.text: Conducts the Caucus-race to dry everyone: marks a circular course, lets all start/stop at will, then declares, 'Everybody has won, and all must have prizes,' and appoints Alice to give the prizes.
facts.argument: "the best way to explain it is to do it"; marked out a circle; "The race is over!"; "Everybody has won, and all must have prizes"; "Why, she, of course," pointing to Alice.

facts.text: Solemnly presented a thimble to Alice with a formal speech and led the group in cheering.
facts.argument: "the Dodo solemnly presented the thimble... 'We beg your acceptance of this elegant thimble;' ... they all cheered.

summaries.text: A sodden bird from the pool who assembles with the others on the bank to get dry.

Dodo, a formal-speaking bird from the pool, proposes a Caucus-race to dry off with others on the bank. Known for his parliamentary tones, he seeks energetic solutions and leads the group in a whimsical meeting.

Dodo, a formal-speaking bird, proposes a whimsical Caucus-race to dry off with others. Known for his parliamentary tones, he leads the group, declaring, 'Everybody has won, and all must have prizes,' and appoints Alice to distribute them.

facts.text: character introduced
facts.argument: "a Lory" is listed among the creatures; Alice argues with it about age.

facts.text: Claims seniority over Alice in an argument, refuses to disclose its age, and turns sulky.
facts.argument: Lory says, "I am older than you"; it "positively refused to tell its age" and "turned sulky."

facts.text: Shivers "Ugh!" during the Mouse's lecture and hastily denies speaking when asked, showing discomfort and defensiveness.
facts.argument: Lory: "Ugh!" then, when Mouse asks "Did you speak?" Lory replies, "Not I!"

summaries.text: A bird among the wet creatures; argumentative with Alice about being older.

facts.text: character introduced
facts.argument: "and an Eaglet" is listed among the creatures in the pool who reach the shore.

facts.text: Objects to long, fancy words and asks for plain English; hides a smile afterward.
facts.argument: "Speak English!... I don't know the meaning of half those long words..." and "bent down its head to hide a smile."

summaries.text: A young eagle among the wet birds gathered on the bank to get dry.

facts.text: character introduced
facts.argument: “an old Crab took the opportunity of saying to her daughter ‘Ah, my dear! Let this be a lesson to you never to lose your temper!’”

summaries.text: An old Crab among the wet creatures; mother of the Young Crab, she admonishes her daughter not to lose her temper.

facts.text: character introduced
facts.argument: “said the young Crab, a little snappishly. ‘You’re enough to try the patience of an oyster!’”

summaries.text: Daughter of the Old Crab; a young crab who snaps back at her mother, showing impatience.

facts.text: character introduced
facts.argument: “one old Magpie began wrapping itself up very carefully, remarking, ‘I really must be getting home; the night-air doesn’t suit my throat!’”

summaries.text: An old Magpie among the birds; leaves the group after Dinah is mentioned, citing the night air as a pretext.

facts.text: character introduced
facts.argument: “a Canary called out in a trembling voice to its children, ‘Come away, my dears! It’s high time you were all in bed!’”

summaries.text: A Canary among the birds; anxious and protective, it gathers its children to leave after Dinah is mentioned.

facts.text: character introduced
facts.argument: “Why, Mary Ann, what are you doing out here? Run home this moment, and fetch me a pair of gloves and a fan!”

facts.text: Housemaid to the White Rabbit; he expects her to fetch his gloves and fan.
facts.argument: Rabbit: “Why, Mary Ann, … fetch me a pair of gloves and a fan!”; Alice: “He took me for his housemaid.”

summaries.text: The White Rabbit’s housemaid; mentioned when the Rabbit mistakes Alice for her and orders 'Mary Ann' to fetch his gloves and fan.

facts.text: character introduced
facts.argument: The White Rabbit calls, “Pat! Pat! Where are you?” and a new voice answers, “Sure then I’m here! Digging for apples, yer honour!”

summaries.text: Pat is a helper summoned by the White Rabbit outside his house. He speaks in a distinctive dialect (saying “arrum” for “arm”), shows reluctance, and is ordered to deal with the giant arm in the window.

facts.text: character introduced
facts.argument: Multiple voices outside the Rabbit’s house mention Bill repeatedly: “Bill’s got the other—Bill! fetch it here, lad!... Bill’s to go down—Here, Bill! the master says you’re to go down the chimney!” Later a “little feeble, squeaking voice” speaks, identified by Alice as Bill.

facts.text: Bill serves as one of the jurors at the trial; after Alice takes his squeaky pencil, he has to write with his finger, which leaves no mark.
facts.argument: “it was Bill, the Lizard” serving as a juror; his squeaky pencil is taken by Alice, forcing him to write with a finger that leaves no mark.

facts.text: As a juror he is referred to as ‘the Lizard’; Alice mistakenly puts him into the jury-box head downwards, leaving him tail-waving and stuck.
facts.argument: “she had put the Lizard in head downwards … the poor little thing was waving its tail … being quite unable to move.”

facts.text: At the trial he resumes writing using ink trickling down his face after being hit with the Queen’s inkstand.
facts.argument: Bill "now hastily began again, using the ink, that was trickling down his face, as long as it lasted."

summaries.text: Bill is a small animal among the White Rabbit’s helpers. He is ordered to go down the chimney to deal with the situation and is kicked back out, later speaking in a feeble, squeaky voice about being sent up like a sky-rocket.

Bill is a small animal and helper of the White Rabbit, known for his feeble, squeaky voice. He is famously kicked out of a chimney and later serves as a juror at Alice's trial, where he struggles to write after Alice takes his pencil.

Bill, also known as 'the Lizard', is a small animal and assistant to the White Rabbit, recognized for his feeble, squeaky voice. He serves as a juror at Alice's trial, struggling to write after Alice takes his pencil, and is humorously stuck in the jury-box head down.

facts.text: character introduced
facts.argument: They are described holding up Bill and giving him something from a bottle after he is blasted out of the chimney.

facts.text: During the trial, one of the pair cheers and is immediately suppressed by the court officers.
facts.argument: "Here one of the guinea-pigs cheered, and was immediately suppressed by the officers of the court."

facts.text: At the Knave of Hearts' trial, the two guinea-pigs cheer and are 'suppressed' by being stuffed head-first into a canvas bag and sat upon.
facts.argument: “Here the other guinea-pig cheered, and was suppressed.” + “They had a large canvas bag… into this they slipped the guinea-pig, head first, and then sat upon it.”

summaries.text: A pair of guinea-pigs who help Bill recover, holding him up and dosing him from a bottle amid the crowd outside the White Rabbit’s house.

facts.text: character introduced
facts.argument: "An enormous puppy was looking down at her..." It barks, plays at chasing a stick, and is big enough to threaten Alice.

facts.text: The puppy is enormous compared to Alice, barks hoarsely, and eagerly chases a stick, making short charges and tumbling in excitement.
facts.argument: "An enormous puppy... barking hoarsely... began a series of short charges at the stick... tumbled head over heels."

summaries.text: A gigantic, playful puppy Alice encounters; yelps and barks hoarsely while chasing a stick. Its great size frightens Alice, who fears being trampled or eaten, and she ultimately flees.

facts.text: character introduced
facts.argument: Alice finds a large blue caterpillar sitting atop a mushroom, smoking a hookah, who addresses her.

facts.text: Displays a curt, contemptuous demeanor; dismisses size changes and future metamorphosis as not confusing, calls Alice back only to advise, 'Keep your temper.'
facts.argument: "You!" said the Caterpillar contemptuously. "Who are you?"; "It isn’t" (about confusion); "Not a bit" (re metamorphosis); "Come back!... I’ve something important to say!... Keep your temper."

facts.text: Commands Alice to recite a poem, harshly judges her recitation as wrong from beginning to end, then pointedly asks what size she wants to be.
facts.argument: “Repeat, ‘You are old, Father William,’”… “It is wrong from beginning to end”… “What size do you want to be?”

facts.text: Exactly three inches high; takes offense at Alice calling three inches a wretched height, then advises that the mushroom's sides alter size (one taller, the other shorter) before crawling away out of sight.
facts.argument: "it was exactly three inches high"; "It is a very good height indeed!" (angrily); "One side will make you grow taller, and the other side will make you grow shorter" ... "Of the mushroom" ... and then it "was out of sight."

summaries.text: A large blue caterpillar perched on a mushroom, arms folded and smoking a long hookah. Speaks in a languid, sleepy voice and is aloof and stern, opening with, 'Who are you?' to Alice.

A large blue caterpillar, known for its aloof demeanor and stern voice, sits on a mushroom smoking a hookah. It dismisses Alice's size changes, commands her to recite a poem, and advises her on altering her size with the mushroom, all while maintaining a curt attitude.

facts.text: character introduced
facts.argument: A large pigeon flew into Alice’s face, beating her with its wings, and screamed, “Serpent!”

facts.text: The Pigeon is hatching eggs in the highest tree and keeps constant watch against serpents, losing sleep for three weeks; it suspects egg-seekers and even considers little girls who eat eggs to be 'a kind of serpent.'
facts.argument: “As if it wasn’t trouble enough hatching the eggs… I must be on the look-out for serpents night and day… I haven’t had a wink of sleep these three weeks… I’d taken the highest tree… they come wriggling down from the sky… if [little girls] do [eat eggs], why then they’re a kind of serpent.”

summaries.text: A large pigeon among the treetops who attacks Alice, screaming “Serpent!” and mistaking her long neck for a snake.

A large, vigilant pigeon hatching eggs in the treetops, mistaking Alice's long neck for a snake and screaming "Serpent!". It has been on high alert for three weeks, viewing egg-seekers, including little girls, as potential threats.

facts.text: character introduced
facts.argument: “a footman in livery came running out of the wood—(she considered him to be a footman because he was in livery: otherwise, judging by his face only, she would have called him a fish)”

summaries.text: A footman in livery with a fish-like face; runs out of the wood and loudly knocks at the door of a small house in a clearing.

facts.text: character introduced
facts.argument: Introduced as another footman in livery with a round face and large eyes like a frog; later called the Frog-Footman and speaks to Alice at the Duchess's door.

facts.text: Sits at the Duchess's door, staring up into the sky; tells Alice there's no use knocking due to noise inside and being on the same side of the door.
facts.argument: "the other was sitting on the ground near the door, staring stupidly up into the sky"; "There’s no sort of use in knocking... because I’m on the same side of the door... they’re making such a noise inside"

facts.text: Stolidly unresponsive and literal-minded; continues speaking calmly despite a plate thrown from inside narrowly missing him.
facts.argument: A large plate skims out, grazing his nose; he continues, "—or next day, maybe," as if nothing happened.

summaries.text: A frog-faced footman in livery at the Duchess's door; repeats a royal invitation and later tells Alice knocking is useless while staring up at the sky.

facts.text: character introduced
facts.argument: "the cook was leaning over the fire, stirring a large cauldron which seemed to be full of soup... There’s certainly too much pepper in that soup!... The only things in the kitchen that did not sneeze, were the cook, and a large cat"

facts.text: Joins in the chorus of the Duchess’s lullaby, shouting "Wow! wow! wow!"
facts.argument: CHORUS: "Wow! wow! wow!" (in which the cook joined)

facts.text: Appears as a witness at the Knave's trial carrying a pepper-box that makes people sneeze; she refuses to give evidence and claims tarts are made of “Pepper, mostly.”
facts.argument: “The next witness was the Duchess’s cook… by the way the people near the door began sneezing… ‘Give your evidence,’ said the King. ‘Shan’t,’ said the cook.… ‘Pepper, mostly,’ said the cook.”

facts.text: Disappears from the courtroom during the confusion and is gone when order is restored.
facts.argument: “by the time they had settled down again, the cook had disappeared.”

summaries.text: The Duchess’s cook, leaning over the fire stirring a cauldron of peppery soup; unaffected by the pepper that makes others sneeze.

The Duchess's cook, known for her resilience to pepper, stirs a cauldron of soup and joins in the Duchess's lullaby with enthusiasm. She appears as a witness at the Knave's trial, carrying a pepper-box and humorously claims tarts are made of 'Pepper, mostly.'

facts.text: character introduced
facts.argument: Alice asks the Duchess why “your cat grins like that,” and the Duchess replies, “It’s a Cheshire cat.”

facts.text: The Cheshire Cat appears sitting on a bough of a tree a few yards from Alice, grinning silently when it sees her.
facts.argument: “…she was a little startled by seeing the Cheshire Cat sitting on a bough of a tree a few yards off. The Cat only grinned when it saw Alice.”

facts.text: renamed to 'Cheshire Cat'
facts.argument: “…she was a little startled by seeing the Cheshire Cat sitting on a bough of a tree…”

facts.text: Claims universal madness in Wonderland and self-identifies as mad; demonstrates the ability to vanish at will.
facts.argument: The Cat: “we’re all mad here. I’m mad.” … “You’ll see me there,” said the Cat, and vanished.

facts.text: Appears good-natured but has very long claws and many teeth; accepts being addressed as “Cheshire Puss.”
facts.argument: “It looked good-natured… very long claws and a great many teeth… ‘Cheshire Puss,’ she began… it only grinned a little wider.

facts.text: Says it growls when pleased and wags its tail when angry, presenting this as proof of being mad; Alice calls the sound purring.
facts.argument: “a dog growls when it’s angry, and wags its tail when it’s pleased. Now I growl when I’m pleased, and wag my tail when I’m angry.” Alice: “I call it purring, not growling.”

facts.text: Can vanish gradually, leaving only its grin visible for a time.
facts.argument: "It vanished quite slowly ... ending with the grin, which remained some time after the rest of it had gone."

facts.text: Can manifest only parts of itself; often appears gradually (grin, then mouth, eyes) and sometimes only as a disembodied head.
facts.argument: “she made it out to be a grin… as soon as there was mouth enough… Alice waited till the eyes appeared… the whole head appeared… no more of it appeared.”

facts.text: When told to be removed, the Cat refused (“I’d rather not”) and was immediately targeted by the Queen for beheading at the King’s request.
facts.argument: “I’d rather not,” said the Cat; the King: “have this cat removed!”; the Queen: “Off with his head!”

summaries.text: The Duchess’s cat, identified as a Cheshire cat; notable for its constant grin that prompts Alice’s question.

The Cheshire Cat, a character from 'Alice's Adventures in Wonderland,' is known for its distinctive, perpetual grin and cryptic advice. Often seen perched on a tree branch, it plays a significant role in guiding Alice through her journey.

The Cheshire Cat from 'Alice's Adventures in Wonderland' is known for its iconic grin and cryptic wisdom. Often seen on a tree branch, it claims to be mad, can vanish at will, and is addressed as 'Cheshire Puss,' guiding Alice through her surreal journey.

The Cheshire Cat from 'Alice's Adventures in Wonderland' is known for its iconic grin, cryptic wisdom, and ability to vanish at will. Often perched on a tree branch, it claims to be mad and is addressed as 'Cheshire Puss,' guiding Alice through her surreal journey.

The Cheshire Cat, also known as 'Cheshire Puss,' from 'Alice's Adventures in Wonderland,' is recognized for its wide grin and ability to vanish at will. It offers cryptic guidance to Alice, claims universal madness, and exhibits a playful yet enigmatic demeanor.

facts.text: character introduced
facts.argument: The scene features “the baby” in the Duchess’s kitchen, being addressed by the Duchess and nearly struck by thrown cookware.

facts.text: Queer-shaped and unruly: limbs splay "like a star-fish," snorts like a steam-engine, and alternately doubles up and straightens out; howls loudly and joins the chorus.
facts.argument: "queer-shaped... like a star-fish"; "snorting like a steam-engine"; "kept doubling itself up and straightening itself out"; CHORUS: "Wow! wow! wow!"

facts.text: While in Alice’s care, the child repeatedly grunts and shows pig-like features; it finally turns into a pig, so Alice sets it down and it trots away into the wood.
facts.argument: “This time there could be no mistake about it: it was neither more nor less than a pig… So she set the little creature down, and… it trot away quietly into the wood.”

summaries.text: An infant in the Duchess’s care; howling amid the chaotic kitchen and nearly struck by flying cookware.

An unruly infant in the Duchess's care, known for howling loudly and chaotic movements resembling a starfish. Often found in the kitchen, dodging flying cookware and adding to the commotion with steam-engine-like snorts.

The Duchess's Baby is an unruly infant known for chaotic, starfish-like movements and loud howling. Often found in the kitchen, it exhibits pig-like features and eventually transforms into a pig, trotting away into the woods.

facts.text: character introduced
facts.argument: The Duchess says, “I must go and get ready to play croquet with the Queen,” indicating a specific Queen exists.

facts.text: Hosts a croquet game today that others plan to attend.
facts.argument: The Cat asks, “Do you play croquet with the Queen to-day?” and adds, “You’ll see me there.”

facts.text: renamed to 'Queen of Hearts'
facts.argument: The Hatter refers to “the great concert given by the Queen of Hearts,” clarifying the Queen’s identity.

facts.text: Hosted a great concert at which the Hatter had to sing.
facts.argument: “…the great concert given by the Queen of Hearts, and I had to sing.”

facts.text: Known for threatening beheading; reportedly told Seven he deserved to be beheaded yesterday.
facts.argument: Five: “I heard the Queen say only yesterday you deserved to be beheaded!”

facts.text: Runs a chaotic croquet game using live hedgehogs as balls and live flamingoes as mallets; stamps about angrily and orders beheadings frequently during play.
facts.argument: "the balls were live hedgehogs, the mallets live flamingoes" … the Queen was in a furious passion … shouting "Off with his head!" or "Off with her head!" about once in a minute.

facts.text: During the croquet game, she screamed with passion and sentenced three players to be executed for missing their turns.
